blocks.content: LRU, least recently used, fixes the central weakness the previous chapter identified in FIFO: it actually pays attention to how pages are being used, rather than blindly evicting whichever page happens to be oldest. Instead of tracking arrival order, LRU tracks how recently each resident page was last touched, and evicts whichever one has gone the longest without being accessed.

This single change, from arrival time to last access time, is grounded in a genuinely important, well established idea in computer systems called locality of reference, and it is exactly what earns LRU a real, measurable, mathematically provable advantage FIFO simply does not have.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409396427-813031409.png
1. The Core Idea: Evict Whoever Was Used Longest Ago
blocks.text: 1. The Core Idea: Evict Whoever Was Used Longest Ago

blocks.content: LRU page replacement makes its eviction decision based on recency of use rather than arrival order. Every time a resident page is accessed, whether by a read or a write, its last used timestamp effectively gets refreshed to right now. When eviction is needed, LRU looks across every currently resident page and removes whichever one has the oldest last used timestamp, the one that has gone the longest without being touched.

This is a genuinely different signal from FIFO. A page that was loaded a long time ago but has been accessed constantly ever since stays safe under LRU, since its last used timestamp keeps getting refreshed, even though FIFO would have marked it for eviction purely for being old.

blocks.title: In one sentence
blocks.content: LRU evicts whichever currently resident page has gone the longest without being accessed, using recency of use rather than arrival order.
2. Why This Works: Locality of Reference
blocks.text: 2. Why This Works: Locality of Reference

blocks.content: LRU is not an arbitrary heuristic, it rests on a genuinely well supported observation about how real programs actually behave, called locality of reference, already introduced briefly in the TLB chapter. Programs tend to access a relatively small, concentrated set of pages repeatedly over any given short stretch of time, loops revisit the same instructions, data structures get accessed again and again in tight succession.

Given this pattern, a page used very recently is genuinely more likely to be used again soon than a page that has sat untouched for a long while. LRU deliberate bet is exactly this: recency of use is a meaningfully useful predictor of near future use, and in practice, for most real workloads, this bet pays off consistently.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409396428-743371080.png
blocks.alt: Why This Works: Locality of Reference

blocks.content: 3. Implementing LRU: Two Classic Approaches

Tracking exact recency for every resident page requires real bookkeeping, and two classic implementation strategies illustrate the tradeoffs involved clearly, even though real systems typically use cheaper approximations covered later in this chapter.
Counter based implementation

Every memory access stamps the accessed page with the current value of a logical clock or counter that increments on every reference. When eviction is needed, the system scans every resident page and picks the one holding the smallest, oldest timestamp.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409396428-542284834.png
Stack based implementation

An alternative implementation maintains an explicit stack of resident page numbers. Every time a page is accessed, it moves, or is inserted, to the top of the stack. Eviction always removes whatever page sits at the very bottom, which is by construction always the least recently used one.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409396428-402244964.png

blocks.content: In this particular reference string, LRU actually produces one more fault than FIFO did with the same 3 frames, a useful, honest reminder that LRU is not universally better on every single input, it is better in the aggregate, on typical workloads exhibiting real locality, and specifically better in one precise, provable structural sense covered next.
5. LRU Never Suffers Belady Anomaly

This is the single most important theoretical fact distinguishing LRU from FIFO. LRU belongs to a mathematically defined family of algorithms called stack algorithms, and it is a proven property of every stack algorithm that adding more physical frames can never increase the total number of page faults, only ever decrease or leave it unchanged.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409396429-862340629.png

This is a genuinely meaningful, structural guarantee, not just an empirical observation from limited testing. It is one of the concrete, well established reasons LRU is generally preferred over FIFO in real system design, even though, as the worked example above shows, LRU is not guaranteed to produce fewer faults than FIFO on every single specific input.
6. The Real Cost: Why True LRU Is Expensive
blocks.text: 6. The Real Cost: Why True LRU Is Expensive

blocks.content: Implementing LRU exactly, as described so far, has a real, practical cost that has to be stated honestly. Updating a timestamp or repositioning a stack entry on every single memory access, not just every page fault, but literally every memory reference a program makes, would impose meaningful overhead directly in the hot path of ordinary program execution.

Because of this real cost, essentially no real operating system implements pure, exact LRU in hardware or software at full fidelity. Instead, real systems use approximation algorithms that capture most of LRU practical benefit at a small fraction of the bookkeeping cost, the most well known of which, second chance, also called clock, is covered in full in the next chapter.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409396717-484488917.png

8. Common Mistakes and Interview Angle

["Assuming LRU always produces fewer faults than FIFO on every possible reference string, when it is only guaranteed never to suffer Belady Anomaly, not guaranteed to strictly beat FIFO on every specific input.","Assuming true LRU is what real operating systems actually implement in practice, when the real bookkeeping cost of exact LRU is why virtually every real system uses an approximation instead.","Confusing locality of reference, the underlying assumption LRU relies on, with a guarantee, it is a strong empirical tendency in typical programs, not a mathematical certainty for every possible access pattern."]
items: Assuming LRU always produces fewer faults than FIFO on every possible reference string, when it is only guaranteed never to suffer Belady Anomaly, not guaranteed to strictly beat FIFO on every specific input.
Assuming true LRU is what real operating systems actually implement in practice, when the real bookkeeping cost of exact LRU is why virtually every real system uses an approximation instead.

Confusing locality of reference, the underlying assumption LRU relies on, with a guarantee, it is a strong empirical tendency in typical programs, not a mathematical certainty for every possible access pattern.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.content: Be ready to explain why LRU is a stack algorithm and therefore mathematically immune to Belady Anomaly, and be ready to explain honestly why real systems approximate LRU rather than implementing it exactly, both are common, substantive follow up questions once FIFO has already been discussed.

LRU fixes FIFO central blind spot by tracking actual usage, at a real implementation cost. The next chapter covers the optimal algorithm, the theoretical best case every practical algorithm, including LRU, is ultimately measured against.
